SENATE DID THE RIGHT THING — AND IT LANDED HARD

If you missed today’s Senate of the Philippines session, here’s a straightforward breakdown of what happened and why it matters.

The session opened with Senator Ronald Bato Dela Rosa moving to dismiss outright the impeachment case against Vice President Inday Sara Duterte, citing constitutional violations — most significantly, the “one-year bar rule” under Article XI, Section 3(5) of the 1987 Constitution, which states:
“No impeachment proceedings shall be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year.”

According to records, 3 impeachment complaints were filed in 2024. The current case — the fourth — was filed in 2025, raising serious questions about whether it violates this one-year prohibition.

Senator Bong Go seconded the motion, pointing out that the impeachment effort does not reflect the true priorities of the Filipino people, especially given the more pressing social and economic issues the country faces.

Then came Senator Koko Pimentel and Senator Risa Hontiveros, who OBJECTED the dismissal. 

Their arguments were the same arguments parroted by yellow-turned-pink legal luminaries kuno saying that the Senate is a “continuing body,” that an impeachment case can carry over the next congress, and the ambiguous use of the word “forthwith” in the Constitution, referring to Article XI, Section 3(6) which says:

“The Senate shall... proceed forthwith with the trial.”

However, these arguments are legal interpretations, not settled doctrine and they didn’t outweigh the constitutional concerns raised by Senator Bato. 

This left Senate President Chiz Escudero with a crucial decision. Some senators proposed that judicial determination be sought to settle the question. But Senator Bato firmly pushed back, stressing that the Senate is sui generis, a unique constitutional body with the sole authority to try impeachment cases, as stated in Article XI, Section 3(6):
“The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment.”

In short: The Senate decides. The courts cannot interfere.

Then, Senator Alan Peter Cayetano proposed a strategic amendment: remand the case back to the House of Representatives, instructing them to address the constitutional defects — especially the violation of the one-year rule— and to clarify whether proper procedures were followed in accepting and endorsing the complaint.

Senator Joel Villanueva agreed which led to voting. 

Results:  18 in favor, 5 against — a strong majority.

Then came Senator Imee R. Marcos, who laid it out the facts behind the impeachment. She itemized the multiple impeachment complaints already filed against VP Sara and questioned the motive behind them. 

She argued that if the real goal were accountability, then let the courts decide, where due process and proof beyond reasonable doubt apply. Impeachment, she reminded everyone, is a political process— one that can be exploited for partisan gain rather than justice.

The message was clear. This isn’t about accountability. It’s about political demolition.

Why this move from Senate matters? 

By remanding the case back to the House of Representatives, the Senate shifts the spotlight. It’s now the HOR, not VP Sara, that will be scrutinized “first.”

They’ll be forced to explain how they sidestepped constitutional limits, and how a fourth impeachment complaint — after three prior filings in the same one-year period — was allowed to pass.

This gives VP Sara Duterte the advantage of discrediting the process before any trial even begins.

The Senate didn’t just follow the Constitution, it exposed the cracks in a political operation.

Checkmate.

And once again, Martin Romualdez’s move backfires. 

Editorial: Tio Moreno
PS|| This is just a summary of the senate session today (June 10, 2025) and a short commentary about what has transpired. I am not reporting news here. Don’t convert this as fake news just because you don’t agree.
